sources.title: When do children learn to tell time?
sources.publisher: Lovevery blog (Team Lovevery), no date shown on the page
sources.quote: Understanding “before” and “after” doesn’t really develop until about 4 years old ... it isn’t until age 7 that your child will understand what yesterday, today, and tomorrow mean. ... A visual timer is a great way to connect the passage of time to something concrete and visible. ... “The timer will beep in five minutes and then we are going to put on our shoes.” ... Describe the actions in terms of order ... occupying your child while they’re waiting for something exciting to happen
sources.supports: A child's sense of tomorrow and soon develops late; visual timers make time visible; describe what happens in order; keep a waiting child busy. A company blog written about toddlers, applied to ages 3 to 5 as general advice.

sources.title: Teaching Children Patience and Waiting Turns
sources.publisher: The Watson Institute, no date shown on the page
sources.quote: Using visual tools like sand timers, countdown clocks, first/then boards, visual schedules ... When the sand in this timer runs out, we will go outside to play. ... Start with short waits, then increase wait times as the child's capacity builds.
sources.supports: Visual tools (sand timer, countdown clock, first then board, visual schedule) and short waits that grow help a child wait.

sources.title: Helping Young Children With Sharing
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (Sarah S. MacLaughlin, 11 Aug 2017)
sources.quote: children this age haven’t developed the ability to put themselves in another’s shoes yet. ... Children this age are focused on their own feelings and thoughts ... an unwillingness to share is perfectly normal at this age! ... It is okay to let children have a “long turn”—a chance to play with the toy—before they share. ... Help the other child wait by offering a different activity. ... a timer or clock can be a helpful rule-keeper and visual aid. ... Once everyone is calm, a short statement about expectations will help children learn new behaviors. ... It’s OK to be upset when you have to wait. Waiting is hard!
sources.supports: Not sharing is normal at this age; a long turn, a timer, a different activity for the waiting child, a short statement once calm, and naming that waiting is hard.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with feelings. The page is about empathy, not about this topic; used only as support for reading stories about a feeling.

sources.title: When do children learn to tell time?
sources.publisher: Lovevery blog (Team Lovevery), no date shown on the page
sources.quote: Understanding “before” and “after” doesn’t really develop until about 4 years old ... it isn’t until age 7 that your child will understand what yesterday, today, and tomorrow mean. ... A visual timer is a great way to connect the passage of time to something concrete and visible. ... “The timer will beep in five minutes and then we are going to put on our shoes.” ... Describe the actions in terms of order ... occupying your child while they’re waiting for something exciting to happen
sources.supports: A child's sense of tomorrow and soon develops late; visual timers make time visible; describe what happens in order; keep a waiting child busy. A company blog written about toddlers, applied to ages 3 to 5 as general advice.

sources.title: Teaching Children Patience and Waiting Turns
sources.publisher: The Watson Institute, no date shown on the page
sources.quote: Using visual tools like sand timers, countdown clocks, first/then boards, visual schedules ... When the sand in this timer runs out, we will go outside to play. ... Start with short waits, then increase wait times as the child's capacity builds.
sources.supports: Visual tools (sand timer, countdown clock, first then board, visual schedule) and short waits that grow help a child wait.

sources.title: Helping Young Children With Sharing
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (Sarah S. MacLaughlin, 11 Aug 2017)
sources.quote: children this age haven’t developed the ability to put themselves in another’s shoes yet. ... Children this age are focused on their own feelings and thoughts ... an unwillingness to share is perfectly normal at this age! ... It is okay to let children have a “long turn”—a chance to play with the toy—before they share. ... Help the other child wait by offering a different activity. ... a timer or clock can be a helpful rule-keeper and visual aid. ... Once everyone is calm, a short statement about expectations will help children learn new behaviors. ... It’s OK to be upset when you have to wait. Waiting is hard!
sources.supports: Not sharing is normal at this age; a long turn, a timer, a different activity for the waiting child, a short statement once calm, and naming that waiting is hard.

sources.title: Helping Young Children With Sharing
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (Sarah S. MacLaughlin, 11 Aug 2017)
sources.quote: children this age haven’t developed the ability to put themselves in another’s shoes yet. ... Children this age are focused on their own feelings and thoughts ... an unwillingness to share is perfectly normal at this age! ... It is okay to let children have a “long turn”—a chance to play with the toy—before they share. ... Help the other child wait by offering a different activity. ... a timer or clock can be a helpful rule-keeper and visual aid. ... Once everyone is calm, a short statement about expectations will help children learn new behaviors. ... It’s OK to be upset when you have to wait. Waiting is hard!
sources.supports: Not sharing is normal at this age; a long turn, a timer, a different activity for the waiting child, a short statement once calm, and naming that waiting is hard.

sources.title: Social Development in Preschoolers: Learning How to Share & Cooperate
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics), last updated 5 Dec 2024
sources.quote: Three-year-olds are able to work out solutions to disputes by taking turns or trading toys. ... Remind them that when two children are sharing a toy, each gets an equal turn. ... However, particularly in the beginning, you'll need to encourage this cooperation.
sources.supports: Taking turns and trading toys, an equal turn for each child, and adults encouraging the cooperation.

sources.title: Getting Preschoolers to Share…How Do You Do It?
sources.publisher: Pathways.org, last updated 18 Jul 2025
sources.quote: If your child has a toy that is their absolute favorite that they do not want to share, put it away before the play date! ... Something visual, like a timer, will let children know exactly when it's time to give up a certain toy. ... Although it's important to talk about taking turns and sharing, seeing it will help too!
sources.supports: Put the favorite toy away before a play date, use a visual timer, and show turn taking as well as talking about it; praise sharing.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with feelings. The page is about empathy, not about this topic; used only as support for reading stories about a feeling.
